title: The Age of the Railway
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: In 1800, the fastest way to travel over land was on horseback, and a journey of a few hundred kilometres took days. Seventy years later, a person could cross a continent by train in a week. The railway was one of the most powerful inventions in history, and it changed not only how people travelled but also how they worked, traded, told the time and thought about distance. Today, high-speed trains run at more than three hundred kilometres an hour and are among the cleanest forms of transport. This passage follows the story of the railway from the first rails to the modern era, and looks at its future.

Railways began long before the steam engine. In mines and quarries, wooden rails had been used for centuries to help horses pull heavy loads, since a wheel running on a smooth rail meets much less resistance than one on a rough road. In the eighteenth century, iron replaced wood. The missing element was a source of power. In 1804, Richard Trevithick built a steam locomotive in Wales which hauled ten tonnes of iron and seventy men along a track, but it was too heavy and broke the cast-iron rails. Several other engineers experimented in the following years.

The decisive step was taken by George Stephenson. His locomotive, Locomotion, pulled the first train on the Stockton and Darlington Railway in England in 1825, and in 1829 his son Robert's engine, the Rocket, won a competition by reaching a speed of about forty-eight kilometres an hour. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, which opened in 1830, was the first line to rely entirely on steam locomotives and to carry both passengers and goods on a regular timetable. Its success sparked a boom, and within twenty years Britain had thousands of kilometres of track.

Railways spread rapidly across the world. In the United States, the first transcontinental line was completed in 1869, when two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah and a ceremonial spike was driven in, reducing the journey from coast to coast from months to about a week. In Russia, the Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891, eventually stretched over nine thousand kilometres from Moscow to Vladivostok. Central Asia was linked by the Trans-Caspian Railway, whose line reached Samarkand in 1888 and later extended to Tashkent, bringing the cities of the Silk Road into a new network.

The railway transformed society. Goods could be carried cheaply and quickly, so that fresh food reached the cities, factories sold their products to distant markets, and farmers could specialise in the crops best suited to their land. Cities grew around stations, and ordinary people could for the first time live in one town and work in another. The need for timetables forced towns to adopt a common time, which led to standard time zones. Railways also created large numbers of jobs, from engineers and drivers to ticket sellers and porters, and they brought news, letters and newspapers to places which had been isolated.

The steam locomotive reigned for more than a century, but its time came to an end. Steam engines were heavy, dirty and wasted most of their energy. From the early twentieth century, diesel and electric locomotives, which are cleaner and more efficient, began to replace them. Electric trains are especially suitable for busy lines since they produce no smoke where they run, and they can be powered from renewable sources. By the middle of the century, many countries were closing branch lines as cars and aeroplanes took passengers and freight, and some people believed that the railway had no future.

The railway has, however, made a comeback. Japan opened the first high-speed line, the Shinkansen, in 1964, and similar networks have since been built in France, Spain, China and many other countries. In Uzbekistan, the Afrosiyob high-speed train connects Tashkent with Samarkand and other cities in a fraction of the time that the journey once took. Dr Peter Lindqvist, a transport economist, argues that on distances between about two hundred and eight hundred kilometres, high-speed trains beat both planes and cars, because they run from city centre to city centre and release far less carbon dioxide per passenger. He expects a new golden age of rail, driven by concern for the climate.
